parole.significato: cheerful, brisk, lively, energetic, sprightly, hale
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian бо́дрый (bódryj), from Old East Slavic бъдръ (bŭdrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ. The reemergence of бо́дрий (bódryj) in modern colloquial Ukrainian most likely occurred under the influence of Russian бо́дрый (bódryj). Doublet of бадьо́рий (badʹóryj).

Inherited from Old East Slavic жалоба (žaloba, “mourning, grief”), from Proto-Slavic *žaloba. The second meaning (complaint) probably developed under the influence of Russian жа́лоба (žáloba, “complaint”).

From Old East Slavic жидъ (židŭ, “Jew”), from Proto-Slavic *židъ. Cognate with Polish Żyd (“Jew”). The offensive connotation of the word is a 20th-century absorption from Russian. In Western Ukraine, євре́й (jevréj) is historically more pejorative than жид (see Khrushchev quote in the Russian entry)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolovortъ. Sense 3 is a calque of Russian коловра́т (kolovrát).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian кꙋшати (kušati, “to taste, to eat”), from Old East Slavic кꙋшати (kušati), from Proto-Slavic *kušati, the sense "to eat" is most likely a semantic loan from Russian ку́шать (kúšatʹ, “to eat”) and was not inherited from Old Ruthenian.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian паха́ти (paxáti), from Old East Slavic пахати (paxati), from Proto-Slavic *paxati. Sense 2 is likely from Russian паха́ть (paxátʹ, “to slave away”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xodę̀ťь. From ходи́ти (xodýty) + -я́чий (-jáčyj). Derived from Russian ходя́чий (xodjáčij), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
